subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 58-year-old man presents 20 hours after the onset of substernal chest pressure. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, and serum troponin I is elevated. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is also elevated, and electrophoresis of LDH isoenzymes is performed to identify the tissue source of the elevation.
question: Which of the following LDH isoenzyme patterns is most likely in this patient?
explanation_correct: LDH exists as five tetrameric isoenzymes composed of H and M subunits; LDH1 (four H subunits) predominates in heart and red blood cells, whereas LDH5 (four M subunits) predominates in liver and skeletal muscle. In healthy serum LDH2 is normally greater than LDH1, but myocardial infarction releases cardiac LDH1 and reverses this ratio, producing a flipped LDH1/LDH2 pattern. The shift appears around 24 to 72 hours after infarction and resolves over several days.

explanation_incorrect.B: LDH2 greater than LDH1 is the normal serum pattern and would not indicate acute myocardial injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: LDH3 is distributed in lung, spleen, and lymphoid tissue and is not the pattern of cardiac injury.
explanation_incorrect.D: LDH4 is not the predominant cardiac isoenzyme, and an LDH4 over LDH5 pattern does not reflect myocardial infarction.
explanation_incorrect.E: LDH5 over LDH4 predominance is seen with hepatocellular injury and skeletal muscle damage, not with myocardial infarction.

educationalObjective: Myocardial infarction releases cardiac LDH1, producing the characteristic flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2 serum pattern, whereas normal serum has LDH2 greater than LDH1.
